name: Philosophy

cells.name: Standing of the sciences and mathematics

objects.label: Being
objects.text: PL.O.A1 Being

objects.label: Ontology and existence
objects.text: PL.O.A1.1 Ontology and existence. Particular and universal; object and property; tropes; substance; mereology; abstract objects against nominalism. Existence answers: materialism, idealism, dualism, neutral monism. These are answers, not further questions.

objects.label: Modality
objects.text: PL.O.A1.2 Modality. Possible worlds as a device; de re and de dicto; essentialism. Rule: a necessity claim must say which type it is: logical, metaphysical or nomological. Modal systems K, T, S4 and S5 as calculi are MA.O.A1; which one models metaphysical necessity is PL.O.A1.2.

objects.label: Causation, persistence and identity
objects.text: PL.O.A1.3 Causation, persistence and identity. Causation answers: regularity, counterfactual dependence, process, interventionist (Woodward 2003). Persistence answers: endurance, perdurance (Lewis 1986).

objects.label: Realism and anti-realism
objects.text: PL.O.A1.4 Realism and anti-realism. Whether the world has a structure apart from our concepts. Putnam's model-theoretic argument assumes that reference is fixed only by total theory plus operational constraints (UNVERIFIED wording). Underdetermination of theory by evidence is cited here from A5.1.

objects.label: Knowledge and mind
objects.text: PL.O.A2 Knowledge and mind

objects.label: Knowledge
objects.text: PL.O.A2.1 Knowledge. The analysis is a deductive group: truth, belief, and a further condition. Truth: a known falsehood is not knowledge.

objects.label: Sources of entitlement
objects.text: PL.O.A2.2 Sources of entitlement. Perception, memory, testimony, reason, introspection. Rationalism and empiricism are answers about source. A priori is a way of being entitled, not a place.

objects.label: Mind
objects.text: PL.O.A2.3 Mind. Identity theory, functionalism, eliminativism, dualism, as answers. Intentionality.

objects.label: Meaning and inference
objects.text: PL.O.A3 Meaning and inference

objects.label: Meaning
objects.text: PL.O.A3.1 Meaning. Reference and sense (Frege's puzzle: "a = a" is trivial, "a = b" can be informative). Use as meaning. Speech acts. Literal and implicated content as concepts.

objects.label: Consequence
objects.text: PL.O.A3.2 Consequence. Deduction preserves truth if valid. Induction does not, and can still be reasonable. Abduction infers to an explanation. Validity is form; soundness adds true premises.

objects.label: Value
objects.text: PL.O.A4 Value

objects.label: Metaethics
objects.text: PL.O.A4.1 Metaethics. Cognitivism, expressivism, realism. The Frege–Geach problem: expressivism must explain how "lying is wrong" keeps its meaning inside a conditional.

objects.label: Normative and applied ethics
objects.text: PL.O.A4.2 Normative ethics, worked descent kept from v1. Key line inductive · answer-families · dimension the bearer of value · order outcome, constraint, character: consequentialism, deontology, virtue ethics.

objects.label: Political and legal philosophy
objects.text: PL.O.A4.3 Political and legal philosophy. Legitimacy of coercion, political obligation, liberty, equality, authority, justice. Owner for PO.O.A1 and LA.O.A1, which cite it.

objects.label: Aesthetics
objects.text: PL.O.A4.4 Aesthetics. What a work is and why it merits attention. Intention, form, reception as answers. Hume's standard of taste (1757). Owner for AR, which applies criteria to named works.

objects.label: Standing of the sciences and mathematics
objects.text: PL.O.A5 Standing of the sciences and mathematics

objects.label: General philosophy of science
objects.text: PL.O.A5.1 General philosophy of science. Explanation, confirmation, law, model, reduction. A model is not the system.

objects.label: Natural sciences
objects.text: PL.O.A5.2 Natural sciences. Philosophy of physics: time, probability in physics, the measurement problem. The formalism stays in PH.

objects.label: Formal sciences
objects.text: PL.O.A5.3 Formal sciences. Philosophy of mathematics: platonism, nominalism, structuralism, as answers to what a theorem is about. The proof stays in MA.

objects.label: Mind and social sciences
objects.text: PL.O.A5.4 Mind and social sciences. Philosophy of cognitive science: representation and explanation in cognitive models. Cites MS.

sections.governing_thought: Philosophy is exhausted by four faces of one pyramid: objects, methods, warrants and bridges. Its objects divide into five claim-types: being, knowledge and mind, meaning and inference, value, and the standing of the sciences and mathematics.
sections.key_line:
Logic inductive · plural noun claim-types · dimension what the question is about · order structural (being, knowing, saying, valuing, the sciences).

1. Being
2. Knowledge and mind
3. Meaning and inference
4. Value
5. Standing of the sciences and mathematics

Phase 2 repair (R7, owner's brief item 3): the earlier draft put the four faces in the key line. The key line is now the Face O partition; the faces are named in the governing thought.
sections.assignment_rules:
1. A claim is placed by the sentence it makes, not by the department or century it comes from.
2. Logic as a claim about consequence is PL.O.A3.2. Calculi and metatheorems are MA.O.A1, cited as "uses MA.O.A1".
3. History of philosophy is reconstruction (PL.M.B5) of answers already placed on Face O. That a philosopher held a view at a date is HI.O.A1; whether the argument succeeds is PL.
4. Philosophy of X: entitlement to assert is A5; what X may enforce or ought to do is A4; what the X-object is, A1 or A2.
5. Philosophy of religion is PL. An argument from premises any reasoner may grant is PL.O.A1.1. Religious epistemology is PL.O.A2.2. The same conclusion argued from a creed is RE.O·T.
6. A moral claim argued from shared premises is PL.O.A4. One citing scripture, creed or school is RE·T. One reporting what a tradition holds is RE·S.
7. Normative legitimacy, obligation and justice are PL.O.A4.3. PO cites them; PO owns who holds power and how (PO).
8. The concept of law is PL.O.A4.3. Whether a norm is valid in a given legal system is LA (W10).
9. Causation in general is PL.O.A1.3. A legal causation test is LA; causal identification from data is EC (EC.B2 design), cited.
10. The hard problem and intentionality are PL.O.A2.3. Processing, measured, is MS.
11. Probability as measure is MA.O.A5; as an agent's choice model, EC.O.A1; its interpretation, PL.O.A5.3.
12. Curry–Howard is CS.O.A1.5; PL.O.A3.2 uses it, with the intuitionistic hypothesis stated.
13. General aesthetic value is PL.O.A4.4. A verdict on a named work is AR.
14. Meaning as a concept is PL.O.A3.1. Meaning in a particular language is LN.O.A3.
15. A tradition enters Face B only as a community of answers. Each non-Western school is named by the claim it makes, never filed as a regional bin.
16. A philosophical claim that contradicts a settled measurement owes that science's warrant, in that science's pyramid.
17. Metaphilosophy (what philosophy is) is this pyramid's master section, not a sixth claim-type.

Coverage. Top level: 5 of 7 land; Philosophy, Misc and Other Academic Areas are refused. Second level: 33 substantive areas, 33 of 33 land (audit had 28 full, 1 partial, 4 missing). Of the 33, five History areas land on a method role, not a cell, and five Tradition areas land on bridges. 16 of 49 are refused: 5 area Misc bins, the 4 Philosophy, Misc entries, and the 7 Other Academic Areas (the audit counted "6 misc bins, 3 non-claim bins", the same 16 split differently; one bin's classification is UNVERIFIED).

Sizes: key line 5; Face O cells 22 (5 A-level + 17 sub-cells: A1 4, A2 3, A3 2, A4 4, A5 4); M roles 5; heuristics 6 (outside count); W rows 22; B bridges 5.

Faces (governing thought): objects, methods, warrants and bridges.

Key-line members, word for word: Being; Knowledge and mind; Meaning and inference; Value; Standing of the sciences and mathematics.
